analysis.one_liner: Sets national emission limits on power plants for four pollutants, including carbon dioxide, using a trading system.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a House floor vote in the 109th Congress; it sat in the Energy and Commerce Committee until that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have capped total annual emissions of sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide from the nation's fossil-fuel power plants, with companies trading emission allowances among themselves. It gave large emission cuts to coal-fired plants but also loosened some existing rules for them, such as the new source review program, in exchange for the certainty of the national caps. The bill was introduced by a Republican with Democratic and Republican cosponsors, referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, sent to its energy subcommittee, and never advanced further.
analysis.who_benefits: People who breathe air downwind of coal- and oil-fired power plants: the bill set declining national caps on sulfur dioxide (acid rain and fine particles), nitrogen oxides (smog), mercury (a neurotoxin that accumulates in fish), and for the first time carbon dioxide, a greenhouse gas [S2] [S3]. Public emissions data would have been reported quarterly and published [S3]. Renewable energy and nuclear plants would have gained, because the bill created reserves of carbon allowances for new renewable units and gave credits for incremental nuclear generation [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Communities downwind of fossil-fuel power plants

how_it_helps.text: Sets national annual tonnage limits for sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide from large fossil-fuel electric generating units, with sulfur dioxide falling to 2.25 million tons a year and mercury to 10 tons a year after 2015 [S3].

Directs the EPA to run allowance trading programs for all four pollutants, with monetary penalties ($5,000 per excess ton of nitrogen oxides, $10,000 per excess pound of mercury, $100 per excess ton of carbon dioxide, adjusted for inflation) and quarterly public reporting of emissions [S3].

Creates a reserve of carbon dioxide allowances for new units and new renewable energy units and gives carbon allowances for incremental nuclear generation, tilting the market toward cleaner generation [S3].
States keep the power to require further cuts from specific plants to fix local air quality problems, and remain free to adopt stricter rules of their own [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners of coal- and other fossil-fuel-fired power plants, who would have had to buy allowances, install pollution controls, or retire dirty units, with some of the cost likely passed to electricity customers [S3]. In exchange, the bill relaxed several existing Clean Air Act requirements for the sector: new source review would apply to far fewer plant upgrades after 2008, plants locating in dirty-air areas after 2009 would not need emission offsets, cost ceilings would limit required control technology, and affected units would be temporarily exempt from mercury hazardous-air-pollutant standards and from visibility protection requirements for 20 years [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Fossil-fuel power plant owners and their customers

drawbacks.text: The bill loosened the new source review program beginning January 1, 2009 so it applied only to new units or changes that increase the maximum hourly emission rate, allowed cost ceilings to limit required pollution-control technology, and removed the offset requirement for new sources in non-attainment areas [S3].

It exempted affected power plants from mercury standards under the hazardous air pollutant program for 8 years and from visibility protection requirements for 20 years, meaning some existing legal avenues for forcing cuts would have been off the table while the caps phased in [S3].

Existing polluters received free allowances allocated in proportion to their past electricity output, and allowance allocations by the EPA could not be challenged in court, which critics could fairly call a grandfathered gift to incumbent emitters [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill was a genuine trade. It locked in large, enforceable national cuts in four pollutants, including the first statutory carbon cap on the power sector, and did it with less litigation and uncertainty than the patchwork it replaced. The price was real: weaker new source review, cost ceilings on required controls, and temporary exemptions from mercury and visibility rules. Whether that trade favored the public depends on whether one trusts the caps to deliver more than the loosened rules gave away; the emission limits were steep, but the giveaway of free allowances to incumbents softened the squeeze on the dirtiest plants.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its energy subcommittee, and no markup, hearing, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Charles Bass of New Hampshire introduced the bill on April 27, 2005, joined by Reps. Davis of Florida, Cooper, and Bradley of New Hampshire as original cosponsors [S1] [S3].
It was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the day it was introduced [S5].
On May 23, 2005, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, and no further action was recorded for the rest of the 109th Congress, which ended January 3, 2007 [S5].
The bill never received a committee vote or a vote by the full House [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Owners of coal-fired power plants and other large fossil-fuel emitters, who avoided binding national caps on mercury and carbon dioxide and kept operating under the existing, more negotiable rulemaking system. People living with power-plant pollution gained nothing.

for.name: Rep. Charles F. Bass
for.role: U.S. Representative, New Hampshire; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Clean Air Planning Act of 2005 to cap four power-plant pollutants, including carbon dioxide.

for.name: Reps. Jim Davis, Jim Cooper, and Jeb Bradley
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, giving it bipartisan sponsorship.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; chaired by Rep. Joe Barton (R-TX) in the 109th Congress
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill; it stayed at the subcommittee stage until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's small sponsoring group was bipartisan (2 Republicans and 2 Democrats at introduction, with cosponsors 2 D and 1 R), but it died in a committee controlled by the Republican majority without any recorded votes, so the partisan shape of the wider House was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have forced steep cuts in sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, mercury, and carbon dioxide, but it cushioned the blow with free output-based allowances, relaxed new source review, and temporary exemptions from mercury and visibility rules. Its interest ran against the public's interest in cleaner air, and the bill's death left it unregulated.

The bill created carbon allowance reserves for new renewable units and credited incremental nuclear generation, giving cleaner generators allowances they could sell. Its success would have coincided with cleaner air for the public.
Binding caps and performance standards for pre-1971 units would have driven demand for scrubbers, mercury controls, and monitoring equipment. None of that materialized.
